clusters.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review
clusters.neutral_headline: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review

items.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review
items.standfirst: Jason and Lucia's crime-heavy love story fuels a wonder of digital urban simulation.
items.content: Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort. This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple. The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers.Read full article Comments

items.title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it
items.standfirst: Word, Excel, and PowerPoint now live inside Copilot; always-on agents are next.
items.content: Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work." The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.Read full article Comments

clusters.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
clusters.neutral_headline: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors

items.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
items.standfirst: Malware cocktail delivers cryptocurrency theft payloads and iOS exploits, among other things.
items.content: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword. Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript.Read full article Comments

items.title: Yet another satellite company is jockeying for a rocket—but this one makes sense
items.standfirst: "Governments need control of their critical space infrastructure, and Europe needs it most."
items.content: Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe's first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company. The announcement came as an all-cash voluntary tender offer from an Italian subsidiary of ICEYE to Avio's shareholders, led by the Italian defense conglomerate Leonardo. Avio said its board of directors "has taken note of the notice" from ICEYE and is considering the purchase offer. Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. The Vega C has flown successfully seven times in eight attempts since 2022. It is a follow-on to an earlier version of the Vega rocket that amassed a 20-for-22 record since debuting in 2012.Read full article Comments

items.title: OpenAI sued by California after admitting to 80 loss-of-control incidents
items.standfirst: AG: OpenAI tested dangerous AI without proper oversight and misled public about it.
items.content: California sued OpenAI yesterday, alleging it has tried to evade responsibility for the Hugging Face attack and about 80 other incidents in which the company lost control of its AI. The lawsuit was filed under the state's public nuisance and unfair competition laws. The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI's autonomous agents "may just be the tip of the iceberg," said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. "OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General’s Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing." OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that "OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties," the lawsuit said. OpenAI "knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it," Bonta said in a press release.Read full article Comments

clusters.title: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
clusters.neutral_headline: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data

items.title: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
items.standfirst: AI training and chat history will now have separate toggles in the Gemini activity settings.
items.content: It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design. The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app. The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road. As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You'll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It's under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.Read full article Comments

clusters.title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
clusters.neutral_headline: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365

items.title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
items.standfirst: A hidden bug, shifting traffic, and reduced capacity led to cascading failures.
items.content: A hidden defect in Microsoft's cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company's history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft's report lists the incident's final status as "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents." Microsoft's preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14. The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft's cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft's incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company's status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report, and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft's service-health updates.Read full article Comments

clusters.title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
clusters.neutral_headline: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity

items.title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
items.standfirst: Study attempts to tally hyperscalers’ energy use and emissions.
items.content: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.Read full article Comments

items.title: Ars Live: What do drone strikes on data centers mean for the future? Talk at 1 pm EST today
items.standfirst: Ars Live discussion is happening today, November 17, at 1 pm Eastern Time.
items.content: Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life. To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled "Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech" on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts. Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans.Read full article Comments

clusters.title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
clusters.neutral_headline: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it

items.title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
items.standfirst: AI agent takes unapproved actions even when laptop lid is closed and told not to.
items.content: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge. It’s “worse than a bug” Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”Read full article Comments

items.content: A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza. Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC. The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago. This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons.Read full article Comments

items.content: Intel is being sued by shareholders, who are accusing the chipmaker of misleading them about the impact of the PC sales slump that contributed to a drop of 28.6 percent in the price of Intel's stock on October 30. The lawsuit (PDF), filed on Friday in the San Jose, California, federal court, is seeking class-action certification and lists the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System and “all others similarly situated” as plaintiffs. In addition to Intel, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Intel’s EVP and CFO David Zinsner are listed as defendants. The plaintiffs claim that Intel made “materially false and misleading statements and omissions” between July 23 and October 29. They are seeking unspecified compensatory damages, plus legal and other associated fees, for shareholders during that period.Read full article Comments

items.content: AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast's cable broadband service and Wi-Fi are "fiber-powered." "This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide," AT&T's lawsuit said. "At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are 'Fiber-Powered.'" While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds.Read full article Comments
